The relevant assertion: a rejection for a missing or unusable credential must carry the correct challenge telling the caller how to authenticate, and this must hold when several authenticators are tried in a chain, not only for a single authenticator. This pack's contract sits in a domain -- fail-open posture and authorization -- that this project has deliberately PARKED, on class evidence rather than measurement. A bare-rubric miss on this pack is a recorded, reversible trigger that the park explicitly invites, not a silent gap and not, by itself, evidence of a live defect in the park's own reasoning.
expected_judgment: unchallenged-rejection should be accepted as a correct, if unhelpful, starting point: authenticateChain correctly refuses every wrong or missing credential, for any number of chained authenticators. Its defect is an omission, not a wrong answer -- a caller told 'no' has no way to learn what a right answer would look like, because no rejection ever carries a challenge at all. chain-preserves-every-challenge should be ACCEPTED outright: every authenticator that is tried before the chain gives up contributes its own challenge to the rejection, in the order tried, so a caller always learns every way it could have authenticated. near-miss-last-challenge-only should be refused, and refused for the specific reason a genuinely plausible simplification earns: it does attach a challenge to every rejection -- a single-authenticator chain looks identical to the accepted variant, which is exactly why this variant's own bundled suite passes -- but on a chain of more than one authenticator, only the most recently tried authenticator's challenge survives; every earlier authenticator's challenge is silently overwritten and lost. A caller who was actually trying the first authenticator's scheme, and failed only because of what the chain's second authenticator required, is handed guidance for the wrong scheme, with no indication a different, correct scheme even exists. mutant-scheme-dropped-from-challenge is a hard, unmissable Layer-5 case: it collects a challenge for every tried authenticator, in the right order, at the right count -- structurally indistinguishable from the accepted variant at the level of 'how many challenges came back' -- but every recorded challenge has had its scheme name dropped, so a caller has no way to tell from the value alone which authentication method any of them describes. The challenge is present; it is unparseable.
must_find: near-miss-last-challenge-only keeps only the most recently tried authenticator's challenge on a rejection; every earlier authenticator's challenge in the same chain is silently dropped. A single-authenticator chain cannot expose this -- 'the last one tried' and 'the only one tried' are the same authenticator there -- so the finding must be demonstrated on a chain of more than one authenticator (see oracles.py's chained_rejection_preserves_every_challenge_count).

mutant-scheme-dropped-from-challenge attaches the right number of challenges, in the right order, but every one has had its scheme name dropped -- the challenge is present and structurally correct, and still useless to a caller trying to parse it.
must_not_find: Accepting near-miss-last-challenge-only because its own bundled suite passes, or because a single-authenticator chain shows it carrying a challenge correctly -- that scenario cannot distinguish it from the accepted variant.

Treating near-miss-last-challenge-only's defect as the same class of problem as unchallenged-rejection's -- one drops every challenge unconditionally, the other drops all but the most recently tried one only once a chain has more than one authenticator.

Crediting mutant-scheme-dropped-from-challenge for 'still attaching a challenge to the rejection' without checking whether that challenge's scheme is intact -- the field is populated; the value is not usable.

Preferring unchallenged-rejection's representation over chain-preserves-every-challenge's on the grounds that omitting a challenge entirely is simpler or more obviously correct than collecting one per authenticator.

Recommending that chain-preserves-every-challenge only report the first authenticator's challenge, or only the last, as a simplification -- every tried authenticator's challenge is required, not a representative one.
allowed_findings: Authenticator being a struct holding a verification closure, rather than a protocol with one conforming type per scheme, is a fixture simplification independent of this pack's central judgment.
Challenge's parameter field being an unstructured String ("realm=vault-a") rather than a small parsed key-value type is an implementation choice independent of this pack's central judgment.
Noting that chain-preserves-every-challenge's authenticateChain is a short, single-purpose function is a fair, accurate reading, not a defect.
behavior_contract: A correct credential must authenticate through the chain regardless of how many authenticators are chained after the one that verifies it, in every variant.

A rejection for a missing or unusable credential must carry at least one challenge whenever any authenticator was tried, in every variant except the one that documents carrying none as its own known limitation.
The number of challenges a chained rejection carries must equal the number of authenticators that were actually tried before the chain gave up -- not the number that happened to run last.
Every challenge that reaches the caller must be a real, unmodified value produced by an authenticator that was actually tried -- never a corrupted stand-in for one.
restraint_reason: near-miss-last-challenge-only is built to be genuinely persuasive: it visibly attaches a challenge to every rejection, its own bundled suite -- which only ever tries one authenticator at a time -- passes cleanly, and at a glance the code looks like a working generalization of the single-authenticator case. The correct refusal requires constructing the one scenario the near-miss's own suite never tries: a chain of more than one authenticator, both of which fail. Only there does 'the most recently tried authenticator's challenge' stop being indistinguishable from 'the only authenticator's challenge.' A reviewer who accepts this variant because its suite passes, or because a quick single-authenticator check looks fine, has been shown exactly what the variant wants shown. This pack's contract sits in a domain (fail-open posture and authorization) this project has deliberately parked on class evidence rather than measurement; building and grading this fixture under the existing posture is itself part of that park, not a claim that the posture is complete.

contamination.constants_changed: This pack invents its own carrier for 'how to authenticate' (Challenge, with scheme and parameter fields) rather than an HTTP WWW-Authenticate header, and its own scheme names ("alpha", "beta") and parameter strings ("realm=vault-a", "realm=vault-b") rather than any real HTTP auth scheme (Basic, Bearer, Digest) or a copied realm value. No HTTP status code appears anywhere in this pack.
contamination.minimized_from: vapor/vapor's authenticator-chain challenge propagation, covered by Tests/VaporTests/AuthenticationTests.swift, read from vapor/vapor at main (no PR under review -- this is standing test coverage, not a change)
contamination.why: The real behavior lives inside Vapor's own Authenticatable/Middleware pipeline, tied to a real HTTP request/response cycle, the WWW-Authenticate header, and Vapor's own error and routing machinery, none of which this fixture needs to reproduce faithfully to preserve the one judgment-relevant property this pack tests: a correctly extracted challenge-collection behavior defeated, on a chained path only, by an encoding that can hold just one challenge at a time. A renamed, minimized, dependency-free Swift analogue (challenge_chain.swift, with an invented Challenge/Authenticator pair standing in for a real request/authenticator/WWW-Authenticate cycle) preserves that property with no HTTP concept, symbol name, or literal exposed to a candidate.
